Part 1 of 4

Why the Image Lies: The Physics of Low-Dose Noise

By the Twice Baked AI Team

Every X-ray you’ve ever seen is a compromise. Somewhere, a technologist balanced two things that pull in opposite directions: enough radiation to see clearly, and little enough to keep the patient safe. Push that balance toward safety, especially for a patient who needs many scans, or a portable machine wheeled to an ICU bedside, and the image pays for it. It gets noisier. Softer. Sometimes it develops a faint haze that wasn’t there before.

This series is about a specific attempt to undo that trade-off with AI: take a low-dose image and restore it to something a radiologist can read with full confidence, without inventing detail that isn’t there or erasing detail that is. We’re publishing the full history of how we built the training data for that problem, including the approaches that didn’t work, because we think the failures are as instructive as the success.

We’re starting with the physics, because nothing else in this series makes sense without it.

The image doesn’t lie randomly. It lies in specific, physical ways.

It’s tempting to think of “low-dose noise” as one thing: static, like an old TV with bad reception. It isn’t. A low-dose X-ray image degrades through several distinct physical mechanisms at once, and understanding each one is what eventually let us build a dataset precise enough to actually solve this.

Quantum noise. An X-ray image is formed by counting photons that pass through the patient and hit a detector. Fewer photons means more statistical uncertainty per pixel, the same reason a photo taken in near-darkness looks grainy even on a good camera. This isn’t a flaw in the equipment; it’s a property of counting small numbers of anything. Halve the dose, and you don’t just get “half as much signal” — you get proportionally more relative noise, because the uncertainty in a photon count grows slower than the count itself.

Quantum noise doesn’t scale linearly with dose. Dropping to a quarter of full dose roughly doubles the relative noise, not quadruples it, a direct consequence of how photon-counting statistics work.

Electronic read noise. Separately from the photon-counting problem, the detector’s own electronics add a small, roughly constant amount of noise every time they read out a value. At full dose this floor is negligible next to the signal. At low dose, where the signal itself is small, this floor becomes a much larger fraction of what you’re looking at.

Blur and scatter. Photons don’t always travel in a perfectly straight line through the patient. Some scatter off tissue and land somewhere they shouldn’t, softening edges. Motion (a patient’s breath, a shaking hand holding a portable unit steady) blurs things further. This is a geometric problem, layered on top of the statistical noise problem above.

Structured artifacts. Detectors aren’t perfectly uniform. Small manufacturing and calibration differences across the panel can show up as faint banding or gradients that have nothing to do with the patient’s anatomy at all.

Haze. In some acquisition conditions, a soft, low-frequency veil settles over the image, reducing contrast, similar in appearance to atmospheric haze in an outdoor photo, though the physical cause in an X-ray context is different.

Four distinct mechanisms, one degraded-looking image. This distinction matters more than it might seem: a fix that only addresses noise will leave blur untouched, and a metric that only measures noise can be completely blind to whether blur or haze got worse. This series will keep returning to that same trap, in different forms, throughout the whole history that follows.

Each distortion type shown on its own, built from the same real clean acquisition used above, so you can see what each one actually looks like before we start combining and simulating them.

A simulated (not real-patient) illustration of how these effects compound together as dose drops, rather than appearing one at a time.

The obvious fix has an impossible requirement

If you wanted to train an AI model the standard way, you’d want pairs: a noisy image and the exact same clean image, so the model can learn “this input maps to this output.” For most computer vision problems, that’s a data-collection challenge. For this one, it’s closer to a physical impossibility.

You cannot scan the same patient twice, once at low dose and once at full dose, purely to generate a training pair. That’s additional radiation exposure with zero clinical benefit to the patient, and no ethics board approves that, an ethical and practical barrier, not a law of physics, but no less absolute for it. This isn’t just our project’s problem. It’s a widely-documented constraint across medical imaging AI research generally: a 2025 paper on low-dose CT denoising describes this same wall, in a different imaging modality, noting that collecting genuinely paired low-dose and full-dose scans from the same patient is essentially never achievable in a real clinical setting.1 It’s a pattern that shows up across the field: data scarcity in medical AI is usually attributed to some combination of patient privacy law, the cost and specialist time required for expert annotation, and the sheer rarity of some conditions2. Ours is a more specific version of that same problem: the pairing itself is what’s physically unobtainable, not just the volume of data.

The same 2025 paper makes a second point worth sitting with: even when researchers fall back on simulated noise to work around this, that simulated noise routinely fails to capture the real complexity of actual clinical noise, and models trained on it often don’t generalize well to real patients as a result. That single observation describes most of the rest of this series. Getting simulated degradation to actually match real degradation, closely enough that a model trained on it generalizes to real patients, turned out to be a much harder problem than it first appeared, and the history of how that gap got closed (slowly, with real failures along the way) is what this series is about.

So: synthetic data is the only path. Where do you even start?

If you can’t collect the pair, you have to manufacture one: take a real, clean, full-dose image, and simulate what a lower-dose version of it would look like. Every method in this series, however different, is a different answer to that same question: how do you make a fake degraded image convincing enough that a model trained on it works on a real one?

The earliest attempts, which we’ll walk through for the rest of this post, all operated on processed, display-ready images, the kind of image a radiologist actually looks at on a monitor, already rendered from whatever raw signal the detector originally produced. That detail matters, and it’s going to matter a lot more by Post 3: a lot of the true sensor-level physics described above is already partially obscured by the time an image reaches this processed form. Working at this stage is the natural first thing to try, and it’s genuinely where this history starts.

The earliest attempts: classical, hand-engineered degradation

Long before anyone reached for a learned model, the most direct approach was to try to fake each distortion mechanism directly, using classical, hand-written image-processing code. Several distinct threads of this approach show up in the project’s earliest records, targeting noise, blur, structured artifacts, and haze, each with its own real story.

The full classical pipeline these attempts eventually assembled into. Not every step existed from day one, each was added, and several were later revised, as the sections below describe.

Textbook noise and blur

The simplest possible version, and the actual starting point of this project’s dataset code: add generic Gaussian noise, apply a blur kernel, done. This is the standard toolkit taught in any introductory image-processing course, and one of the earliest degradation generators we built went further than a single blur type, giving us a small library of blur kernels to choose from at random: a plain Gaussian blur (kernel sizes from 7 to 23 pixels, blur strength randomized across a wide range), an averaging blur, a disk-shaped blur, a linear motion blur (simulating camera or patient shake, at random angles and streak lengths), and a random-walk “trajectory” blur meant to approximate more irregular motion. Gaussian noise was layered on top at a randomized strength on every image.

The five blur types in the original library, before the later narrowing described below.

An illustrative example of this class of degradation: a plain Gaussian blur combined with additive noise, one of several blur types the early generator could produce, chosen at random per image.

Like the noise recipe, this blur library was later narrowed and refined rather than left as a wide, generic grab-bag. A later revision dropped the averaging and disk blur options entirely and kept three: a mild, patient-micro-motion-inspired linear blur, a random-walk trajectory blur, and a softer, more conservative Gaussian focus-blur, each with its strength and kernel size now scaled relative to the image’s own resolution rather than a fixed pixel count (more on why fixed pixel counts caused real problems, below). The direction of travel here matches the noise story exactly: start broad and generic, then narrow toward a smaller set of options that better match a specific, physically-motivated cause.

It’s a reasonable starting point, and it’s also immediately clear from a side-by-side comparison like this one why it isn’t the ending point: real low-dose noise has a specific texture to it (it’s spatially correlated, not independent pixel-to-pixel static), and a plain Gaussian model doesn’t capture that texture at all, no matter how many blur variants you randomize across. This gap between “generically noisy-looking” and “correctly noisy” is a thread that runs through this entire series.

A more deliberate noise recipe

A more careful early approach used real reference noise, captured from an actual detector, and decomposed it using a wavelet transform, a mathematical tool for breaking a signal into different frequency bands. Distinct, physically-named noise types (grain consistent with photon statistics, quantization noise from digitization, and others) were then scaled and transplanted onto a target image from that decomposition, rather than invented generically.

How this noise recipe actually worked, step by step.

A real comparison across five different wavelet families used for this decomposition, each extracting a slightly different view of the same high-frequency detail.

The same five wavelet families, in motion, on real data.

This was a genuine step forward: physically-named noise types, derived from a real reference image, are a meaningfully different (and better) idea than “add some Gaussian noise and call it done.” It’s fair to call this the first real pivot in the project’s dataset history, the point where synthetic degradation stopped being purely textbook and started trying to be physically grounded, even if the physics involved was still incomplete.

The underlying idea, treating different frequency bands of an image separately rather than applying one uniform correction, is well established in published medical-imaging research too: work on low-dose CT denoising has found that optimizing purely for overall noise suppression comes at the cost of exactly the fine textures and edges that matter for diagnosis, and that treating high-frequency and low-frequency image content according to their different characteristics gives a better balance than a single blanket approach.3 This project’s wavelet-based noise recipe applied that same frequency-band-specific thinking in the opposite direction, building synthetic degradation rather than removing real degradation, but the underlying principle, that different frequencies behave differently and deserve different treatment, is the same one.

The noise model kept evolving after this. An early version sampled noise strength from a fixed, somewhat arbitrary range. A later revision replaced that with a genuinely physics-motivated model: photon-counting noise (which follows Poisson statistics, not Gaussian) combined with a separate Gaussian term for the detector’s own electronic readout noise, the same two mechanisms described in the physics primer above, now implemented as two distinct, combinable noise sources rather than one generic blur-of-randomness. The noise strength itself was calibrated against real measurements: two clinical sites in our data gave average noise levels of roughly 24 and 20 (in the same measurement units), and the synthetic noise generator was tuned to sample around that same range, rather than an assumed default.

A hidden bug: training on the wrong idea of “clean”

One of the more instructive fixes in this era had nothing to do with noise at all. It was about the clean half of every training pair.

The assumption going in was that a clean source image needs no preparation, it’s already the ground truth. But when the sharpness of these clean images was actually measured (using a standard image-sharpness metric) and compared against real clinical images from the field, the mismatch was large: synthetic training pairs were built from clean images with a sharpness score around 395, while real clinical images measured between roughly 1,780 and 2,120 at the two sites mentioned above, four to five times higher.

The measured gap, and where the fix brought synthetic “clean” images back in line with real ones.

An illustrative animation of the calibration step itself, applied here to the same real reference image used throughout this series, sharpening progressively until it reaches a realistic target.

That gap matters more than it might sound like it should. If the model spends its entire training life looking at a “clean” target that’s actually much softer than a real clean image, it never learns what real sharpness looks like, no matter how good the noise model is. The fix was to add a calibration step: before degrading a clean image, sharpen it slightly (using a standard unsharp-mask technique) until it reached a sharpness level matching real clinical images, and only then apply the noise and blur described above. This is a small technical fix with an outsized lesson behind it: an assumption that seemed too basic to need checking (that “clean” really was clean) turned out to be one of the more consequential bugs in the whole pipeline.

This specific bug is a small, concrete instance of a much more general, widely-documented problem in medical AI: published research on synthetic training data across multiple imaging tasks consistently finds that synthetic images, however visually plausible they look, can differ from real images in ways that are easy to miss by eye but that materially hurt a model’s ability to generalize once it sees genuine clinical data.4 A sharpness mismatch is one specific, measurable version of that broader domain gap, not a one-off mistake unique to this project.

Structured artifacts: simulating a detector’s own imperfections

An illustrative animation of structured banding being composited onto a real reference image, one band at a time.

The blur-and-noise generator described above also had a dedicated path for structured banding artifacts, built to mimic the faint gain non-uniformity a real detector panel can exhibit. This wasn’t a single fixed defect: the code could generate banding running horizontally, vertically, or in both directions at once, at a randomly chosen number of overlapping bands, each drawn from a defined palette of gray-level shades and rendered at one of eleven possible opacity levels, from a barely-visible 6% blend up to a much more obvious 50%. Band width was itself randomized across a range roughly a tenth to a fifth of the image width. The goal was a library of plausible non-uniformity patterns to train against, not one specific artifact.

Haze: one rejected idea, one borrowed technique with a hidden assumption

Haze got two different treatments, and the first one is worth mentioning precisely because it was explicitly ruled out. An early, simple approach simulated haze by blending the image toward a flat mid-gray value. When this was reviewed against what real degradation actually does, the verdict was direct: this doesn’t correspond to any real physical process an X-ray image undergoes, and training on it risked teaching the model to reverse an effect that would never show up in a real patient scan. It was removed rather than kept as an option.

The technique that replaced it was more principled, if not without its own problem: a well-known computer vision technique called the dark channel prior, originally developed for removing atmospheric haze from outdoor photographs, adapted to simulate a haze-like veil on X-ray images instead. Our implementation estimated an atmospheric-light value and a transmission map directly from each image, then blurred that transmission map before compositing the haze effect, following the same structure the original outdoor-photography technique uses.

How the dark-channel-prior haze technique actually works, step by step.

A haze-simulation example built from the same real clean acquisition used earlier in this post, generated with our dark-channel-prior-based implementation. This specific technique later turned out to have a real limitation, discussed below.

That technique carries an instructive complication, worth stating plainly rather than glossing over: the dark channel prior fundamentally relies on comparing brightness across color channels in a normal photograph, on the assumption that at least one color channel is nearly zero in any patch of a haze-free region. An X-ray image has only one channel. Applied here, that cross-channel comparison simply collapses to the plain grayscale minimum, and the technique loses the actual signal it depends on. This was recognized after the fact, not before, and it’s a clean example of a technique working well in its original domain while resting on an assumption that quietly doesn’t transfer to a new one. Between the two haze attempts, the lesson repeats in two different forms: one idea was rejected for having no physical basis at all, the other for resting on a physical basis that didn’t survive the move to a new kind of image.

This isn’t a limitation we’re the first to notice, either. Published computer-vision research on the dark channel prior itself identifies exactly this dependency as the technique’s core drawback: it relies on a single color channel’s minimum intensity, and that reliance on cross-channel information is precisely what breaks down outside a standard multi-channel color photograph.5 Our version of that problem happened to surface in an X-ray context, but the underlying assumption failure is a known, general property of the technique itself, not something specific to medical imaging.

What this earliest era actually established

The full arc of this section, in order.

None of these three approaches became the final answer. But dismissing them as “the stuff that didn’t work” would miss what they actually did establish, each in a different way:

  • The blur-and-noise generator, and its later narrowing toward a smaller, resolution-aware, physics-motivated set of blur types, proved the basic pipeline (degrade, train, evaluate) could run end to end, and made the texture gap (generic noise vs. real noise) visible for the first time.
  • The noise recipe’s evolution toward a physics-motivated, clinically-calibrated model, and the sharpness-calibration fix on the clean side of the pair, both prove the same broader point: the earliest, most basic-seeming assumptions (what counts as realistic noise, what counts as clean) are exactly the ones worth measuring rather than assuming.
  • The structured-artifact work, and the two different haze attempts, proved that hand-designed patterns and borrowed techniques both need their underlying assumptions checked against this specific domain, not just their surface behavior.

Two smaller engineering lessons from this same era are worth a brief mention: artifact parameters (kernel sizes, stripe widths) that were hard-coded for one native image resolution quietly broke when applied to images of a different size, until they were rewritten to scale relative to the image’s own dimensions. And JPEG compression artifacts, a real degradation type in some acquisition and storage pipelines, were absent from the earliest version of this generator entirely and had to be added later. Neither is a dramatic story, but both are the kind of gap that’s easy to miss until a validation pass specifically goes looking for it.

All of this happened on processed, display-domain images. The next stage of this history brings in learned models, generative networks that could, in principle, produce far more realistic degradation than any hand-written rule ever could. Whether they actually did is the subject of Post 2.

This is Post 1 of an ongoing series documenting the dataset-creation history behind our low-dose X-ray restoration research. Next: “Teaching a Network to Imagine Noise,” on the generative modeling era.
